sequence_index values are drawn from this block's private band 3000-3099 and are ORDERED, not final; the topological renumbering pass re-seats them into the final 1..154.
gr_aux_system is taught as ONE mechanism - move the helper to ask, put not after it to refuse, fetch do when the sentence has none - because eleven later points depend on it.

Judgement call flagged for the verify agent: gr_questions_wh is a choice point (R1's delta column) but the closed 19-value confusion-set list has no set for the subject/object question split. points.title: Saying what usually happens, and what is true whether anyone is watching or not

teach.can_do: I can say what I do regularly and what holds true all the time.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the first thing anybody asks you about, and the shape you will use more than any other in speech and in writing.
teach.meaning: The plain verb is English's way of saying that something is not news. It is what happens over and over, what holds true whether or not anyone is watching, and what a person or a place simply does. It does not put your listener at the scene. It hands them the shape of things instead of the picture in front of you, so it covers yesterday and next month as easily as it covers this afternoon.

form.pattern: subject + plain verb, and the verb takes -s when the subject is one person or one thing
notes: one person or one thing takes the -s: the ferry leaves, my sister paints
you, we, they and any group of people or things take the plain verb: the ferries leave
the -s belongs on the verb and never on the word in front of it
form.negative: subject + do not or does not + plain verb
form.question: Do or Does + subject + plain verb ...?

spec.caption: Not one dot near now, but a row of them either side of it. That row is what the plain verb claims.

worked_example.sentence: The Sandmouth ferry leaves the harbour at ten past six.
worked_example.why_this_form: This is the timetable rather than this morning. The plain verb says the ferry does it whenever there is a ferry to run.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Is leaving would stand you on the quay watching one boat pull away, and would tell you nothing about tomorrow.

notice_set.sentence: Rosa cycles to the depot.
notice_set.question: Did she cycle there this morning?
notice_set.why: It reports what she does as a rule, and a rule leaves room for an exception on any one morning.

notice_set.sentence: The Norland library opens at nine.
notice_set.question: Can you get in at half past eight?
notice_set.why: Nine is when the doors go back, every day, so half past eight is too early on all of them.

notice_set.sentence: Salim works nights.
notice_set.question: Is he at work at this minute?
notice_set.why: Nights are his pattern. Whether he is on shift while you read this is outside what the sentence claims.

notice_set.sentence: The water in the Verdon runs low in August.
notice_set.question: Does this happen in most Augusts?
notice_set.why: The plain verb reports the habit of the river rather than one particular dry summer.

notice_set.sentence: Halima teaches two evening classes.
notice_set.question: Is she in a classroom as you read this?
notice_set.why: Two evening classes is her arrangement. The sentence never puts her in a room at any given hour.

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this what generally happens, rather than what is going on around me?
teach.false_rule: That the plain verb means the present. It means the pattern, and a pattern reaches back into last year and forward into next.

errors.wrong: My brother work at the Ashfield depot.
errors.right: My brother works at the Ashfield depot.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has built the sentence correctly and then run out of attention before the ending. Nothing in the meaning needs the -s, so nothing reminds them it is missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: s on work.
errors.l1_note: Plenty of first languages mark person on the verb by other means, or not at all.

errors.wrong: The two lifts in the tower needs a service every spring.
errors.right: The two lifts in the tower need a service every spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Tower sits directly in front of the verb and it is one thing, so the ending attaches to the nearest noun instead of to the two lifts that the sentence is actually about.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on needs.

errors.wrong: Every Tuesday the crew is checking the fire doors.
errors.right: Every Tuesday the crew checks the fire doors.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner pictures the crew at work and describes the picture. Every Tuesday is a pattern, and a pattern has no picture to describe.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is checking becomes checks.

errors.wrong: Halima runs the harbour cafe and she opened at seven.
errors.right: Halima runs the harbour cafe and she opens at seven.
errors.why_it_happens: Each verb was chosen on its own. The first half sets up a standing arrangement and the second half quietly reports one morning, and nobody reads the two together.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: opened becomes opens.

pays_in.note: Every answer about your job, your home or your week is built out of it.
pays_in.model: I work for a small firm that fits out shop interiors.

pays_in.note: General statements about how things stand run on the plain verb.
pays_in.model: Most coastal towns depend on a single bus route into the nearest city.

pays_in.note: A passage explaining how a system works stays in it, so a stem that leaves it is doing something.
pays_in.model: The scheme charges drivers by the hour rather than by the journey.

used_in.quote: What do you do? is the first question on the card, and the answer cannot be built without this.

payload.sentence: Omar drives the school minibus.
payload.question: Is he behind the wheel as you read this?

feedback.why_key: The plain verb hands you his job, not his afternoon. Where he is at this minute is a different question that nobody has answered.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the plain verb as a pattern, never as a snapshot.

payload.sentence: The Brackenfield market closes at two on Wednesdays.
payload.question: Will it be shut next Wednesday afternoon?

feedback.why_key: A standing arrangement covers the Wednesdays that have not arrived yet, which is exactly what makes this shape useful.
feedback.feed_forward: Carry the pattern forward to any day that fits it.

payload.context: Ines is telling a new colleague about her family.
payload.sentence: My sister work for the ferry company.
reasons: the verb is missing the ending that one person takes
the sister does not work there
the wrong verb has been chosen
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One sister is one person, and English puts an -s on the verb for one person. The meaning is clear and the ending is still missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the people in front of the verb before you leave it.

payload.context: From a leaflet about the harbour service.
payload.stem: The first boat ___ (reach) Norland before the shops open.

feedback.why_key: One boat, so the verb takes the ending. The leaflet is describing what happens on any ordinary morning.
feedback.feed_forward: Add -es after a verb ending in ch, sh, s or x.

payload.context: Two neighbours comparing their weeks.
payload.stem: My knees ___ (ache) after a long shift, so I ___ (swim) on Sundays.

feedback.why_key: Two knees and one I, and neither of them takes the ending. Both halves report a regular week rather than one bad Sunday.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb plain after I, you, we and they.

payload.context: Open a paragraph about how Marlow is laid out.

expected: most of the town relies on one bridge

feedback.why_key: Most of the town is one thing taken as a whole, so the verb takes the ending, and the sentence states a standing fact about the place.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat most of the town as one thing, not as many people.

payload.given: Kester is sorting parcels. He does this on every shift he works.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that reports the job rather than the moment.

expected: sorts parcels on every shift he works

feedback.why_key: Once the sentence is about every shift, there is no single moment left to picture, and the plain verb is what carries that.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the -ing shape when the sentence covers every occasion.

payload.audio_text: The ferry leaves at six and reaches Norland by seven.

expected: the ferry leaves at six and reaches norland by seven

feedback.why_key: The two endings are the quietest sounds in the sentence and they are the only thing marking the subject. If you cannot hear them you will not write them.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the last sound of each verb, not the first.

payload.sentence: The college takes on forty apprentices every autumn and placed them with local firms.

feedback.why_key: The first half sets up something the college does every year, and the second half quietly shrinks it down to one autumn that is over.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the verbs of a sentence together before you leave it.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about commuting costs.
payload.sentence: The price of the season tickets rise faster than wages.
reasons: the ending belongs to the price, not to the tickets
the prices are not rising at all
the wrong verb has been chosen
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One price is doing the rising. Tickets is simply the nearest word, and the verb has attached itself to the wrong one.
feedback.feed_forward: Find what is doing the verb, then ignore everything between.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody has asked what you do. Write one sentence about the work or study you do in an ordinary week, not about what you happen to be doing today.

feedback.why_key: An ordinary week has no single moment in it, so the plain verb is the only shape that fits what you were asked.
feedback.feed_forward: Describe the week, not the afternoon.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about work or study. Give a thirty-second answer about what you do in an ordinary week. Record it, then listen back and mark every verb that lost its ending.

feedback.why_key: Under speaking pressure the ending is the first thing to go, because it carries no meaning and costs attention you are spending elsewhere.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen back and count the endings you dropped.

points.title: Putting the small -s on the verb when one person or one thing is doing it

teach.can_do: I can add the -s whenever a single doer is behind the verb, and I can say it out loud.
teach.why_it_matters: It stays wrong for months after you know the rule. That is normal, and it is why this one comes back more often than the others.
teach.meaning: This ending carries almost no meaning. Nothing is lost when it goes missing, which is exactly why it goes missing. It is a marker of agreement: it ties the verb back to the one person or one thing doing it, so a listener knows the sentence is about your sister rather than your sisters. Because it means so little, no picture in your head reminds you to add it. Only practice does.

form.pattern: verb + -s when the doer is one person or one thing that is not you and is not the person you are speaking to
notes: add -es after ch, sh, s, x and z: watches, pushes, misses, fixes
a y sitting behind a consonant gives way to -ies: carries, tidies, hurries
have becomes has, do becomes does, go becomes goes
the ending has three sounds: a hiss after p, t, k and f, a buzz after most other sounds, and an extra syllable after ch, sh, s and x
form.negative: The ending moves onto does not, and the main verb loses it: she does not carry.
form.question: It moves onto does in a question too: does she carry?

rungs.text: she stops, he laughs, it drifts
she leaves, he calls, it rains
she watches, he pushes, it misses

spec.top_label: an extra syllable, after ch, sh, s and x
spec.bottom_label: a quiet hiss, after p, t, k and f

worked_example.sentence: Halima carries the takings to the bank on a Friday.
worked_example.why_this_form: One person is doing the carrying, so the verb ties itself back to her, and the y at the end of carry gives way to -ies.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Carry with nothing on the end would point at a group, and a reader would start looking for the other people who are not there.

notice_set.sentence: Ines locks the yard gate at six.
notice_set.question: How many people are doing the locking?
notice_set.why: The small ending on the verb is the only thing in the sentence telling you it is a single person.

notice_set.sentence: The wardens lock the yard gate at six.
notice_set.question: How many people are doing the locking?
notice_set.why: The plain verb points away from a single person, and the word in front of it names a group.

notice_set.sentence: My cousin watches the yard while we load.
notice_set.question: How many people are watching the yard?
notice_set.why: Watches is an extra beat longer than watch, and that extra beat is doing all the work.

notice_set.sentence: The engine misses on cold mornings.
notice_set.question: Is the sentence about one engine or several?
notice_set.why: The ending after ss adds a whole syllable, so a listener hears it even in a noisy yard.

notice_set.sentence: Salim and his brother share the early run.
notice_set.question: How many people are sharing the run?
notice_set.why: Two people joined by and make a group, and a group leaves the verb plain.

teach.rule_line: One person or one thing doing it: put -s on the verb.
teach.false_rule: That the ending belongs to the noun. Add it to the noun and you have two of something; add it to the verb and you have one.

errors.wrong: Ines finish at four on a Thursday.
errors.right: Ines finishes at four on a Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: The ending carries no meaning, so nothing in the picture the learner is building calls for it. It is dropped under any load at all, long after the rule is known.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: es on finish.

errors.wrong: My cousin carrys the boxes up on his own.
errors.right: My cousin carries the boxes up on his own.
errors.why_it_happens: The rule has been remembered and applied straight to the spelling on the page. A y sitting behind a consonant behaves unlike a y behind a vowel, and nothing on the page flags the difference.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: y becomes ie.

errors.wrong: The cost of the repairs worry my parents.
errors.right: The cost of the repairs worries my parents.
errors.why_it_happens: Repairs is the last thing the learner read before reaching the verb, so the verb agrees with it. The word actually doing the worrying is four words back.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: es on worry.

errors.wrong: She go to the market before her shift.
errors.right: She goes to the market before her shift.
errors.why_it_happens: Go is one of the first verbs anybody learns and it is stored whole, in its plain shape, so the ending never got attached to it in the first place.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: es on go.

pays_in.note: Talking about anyone in your family means one person doing something, over and over.
pays_in.model: My aunt runs a small guest house and my uncle does the accounts.

pays_in.note: A general claim about one group or one system needs it in every sentence.
pays_in.model: A well-planned bus network keeps a town moving when the roads fail.

pays_in.note: That ending is frequently the sole clue to how many people are meant.
pays_in.model: The warden checks the gate, and the drivers check the load.

used_in.quote: Answers about a home town are full of single places doing single things, and every one of them needs the ending.

payload.sentence: My aunt fixes the nets before the season starts.
payload.question: How many people fix the nets?

feedback.why_key: The extra syllable on fixes is the only marker in the sentence, and it points at a single person.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the doers from the ending on the verb.

payload.sentence: The list of empty flats grows every month.
payload.question: What is doing the growing?

feedback.why_key: The ending ties the verb to the list itself, and the flats are merely standing alongside. One list, one ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the ending back to the word it belongs to.

payload.context: Dev is talking about his grandmother.
payload.sentence: She live on the far side of Marlow.
reasons: one person is doing it and the verb has no ending
the grandmother has moved away
the wrong verb has been chosen
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Everybody understands the sentence, and that is the trouble: nothing about the meaning pushes back when the ending goes missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the verb aloud and listen for the ending.

payload.context: From a letter to a friend about your household.
payload.stem: My youngest brother ___ (tidy) the kitchen and nobody else ___ (touch) it.

feedback.why_key: Both doers are single. The y after a consonant gives way, and touch takes the longer ending because of the ch.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the last two letters of the verb before adding anything.

payload.context: Talking about a market stall you like.
payload.stem: The woman on the corner ___ (do) a soup that ___ (cost) almost nothing.

feedback.why_key: Do turns into does, and the soup is one thing, so the verb after it takes the ending as well.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn does and goes as spellings, not as rules.

payload.context: From a paragraph about renting.
payload.stem: The shortage of small flats ___ (push) rents up across the whole district.

feedback.why_key: One shortage is doing the pushing. Flats is simply the nearest word, and nearness has no vote here.
feedback.feed_forward: Skip back over of and everything after it.

payload.context: Say what one person in your family does most evenings.

expected: my father watches the boats from the wall

feedback.why_key: One father, so the verb carries the ending, and after the ch it arrives as a whole extra beat.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the finished sentence aloud before you submit it.

payload.given: Good teachers notice when a pupil has stopped following.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that it is about one teacher rather than about teachers as a group.

expected: notices when a pupil has stopped following
notices when a pupil has stopped following.

feedback.why_key: Moving from a group to a single person moves the ending from the noun onto the verb, which is the whole trade this point is about.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the -s from the noun to the verb.

payload.audio_text: She catches the early bus and misses the worst of it.

expected: she catches the early bus and misses the worst of it

feedback.why_key: Both endings arrive as a full extra syllable here, which makes this the easiest place to hear a marker you usually cannot.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the syllables in each verb as you write it.

payload.sentence: The population of the coastal towns fall every winter and recovers in May.

feedback.why_key: The second verb in the sentence got it right. The first one agreed with towns because towns is what the eye had just passed.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the doer, then jump straight to the verb.

payload.context: From a note about equipment on the estuary.
payload.sentence: Each of the sensors send a reading every hour.
reasons: each points at one sensor at a time, so the verb needs the ending
the sensors are not sending readings
the wrong verb has been chosen
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Each picks the sensors off one by one. However many are out there, the verb is only ever dealing with one of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat each and every as one, whatever follows them.

payload.context: Two lines lifted from different pages of the same yard logbook.
meanings: One person is responsible for it.
It is shared out among several people.

feedback.why_key: One small letter moves from the verb to the noun, and the number of people responsible changes with it. Nothing else in either line differs.
feedback.feed_forward: Read where the -s sits before you decide how many.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences to a friend about one person in your household and what they do on an ordinary weekday. Keep both sentences about that one person.

feedback.why_key: Two sentences about one person means two chances to drop the ending, which is roughly the rate at which it is dropped in real writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Check both verbs before you send it.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 2 card about a long-running hobby. Speak for a minute about someone else who does it, so every verb is about one person. Record it and count the endings you lost.

feedback.why_key: A minute of speech about one person is the hardest place to hold this ending, because attention is going to content and the ending is worth nothing.
feedback.feed_forward: Play the recording back and mark every missing ending.

points.title: The one move behind every question and every negative in English

point_json.grammar_name: The auxiliary system: helper verbs and do-support

teach.can_do: I can turn any statement into a question or a negative with one move, and I know which move it is.
teach.why_it_matters: Learn it once here and you have already learned questions, negatives, short answers, tag questions and eleven later points. Skip it and you learn each of them separately.
teach.meaning: English keeps a small crew of helper verbs, called auxiliaries: am, is, are, have, has, can, will and a few more. They carry the jobs the main verb is not allowed to do. To ask, the helper hops in front of the person doing it. To say no, the word not goes straight after the helper. And when a sentence has no helper of its own, do or does arrives to be one, takes the ending, and hands the main verb back its plain shape.

form.pattern: helper + subject + plain verb = a question; subject + helper + not + plain verb = a negative
notes: am, is, are, have, has, can and will are already helpers, so nothing new is needed
when there is no helper, do or does arrives to do the job
the helper takes the -s and the main verb goes plain: does she work, never does she works
in speech the helper and not squash into one word: don't, doesn't, isn't, aren't, can't
form.negative: put not straight behind the helper; if the sentence has none, fetch do or does first
form.question: helper + subject + plain verb ...?

left.text: The harbour office opens on Saturdays.

right.role: the same words with a helper brought in to do the work
right.text: Does the harbour office open on Saturdays?

spec.caption: One move, and it is the same move in every question, every negative and every short answer you will ever build.

worked_example.sentence: Does the harbour office open on Saturdays?
worked_example.why_this_form: The statement had no helper of its own, so does arrives, hops to the front, and takes the ending off open on its way past.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The harbour office opens on Saturdays, with the same words in their first order, is somebody telling you the answer rather than asking for it.

notice_set.sentence: Does Rosa drive the early van?
notice_set.question: Does the speaker already know the answer?
notice_set.why: Putting a helper in front of Rosa is how English signals that the speaker is short of the answer.

notice_set.sentence: Rosa doesn't drive the early van.
notice_set.question: Is Rosa behind the wheel of the early van?
notice_set.why: Not sits directly after the helper and cancels everything that comes after it.

notice_set.sentence: Is the warden here on a Sunday?
notice_set.question: Did the speaker need to bring in an extra word to ask this?
notice_set.why: Is was already a helper, so it simply moved to the front. Nothing had to be fetched.

notice_set.sentence: The lifts don't stop at the top floor.
notice_set.question: Can you reach the top floor in a lift?
notice_set.why: The helper is doing the refusing, which is why the main verb behind it stays in its plain shape.

notice_set.sentence: Can Salim open the yard gate?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about something Salim is able to do?
notice_set.why: Can was already a helper and moved to the front on its own, exactly as is and are do.

discovery.prompt: The sentences on the left are statements and the ones on the right ask about the same thing. What happened on the way across?
pairs: The harbour office opens on Saturdays.
Does the harbour office open on Saturdays?
Salim can open the yard gate.
Can Salim open the yard gate?
The wardens check the bins.
Do the wardens check the bins?

candidate_rules.text: A helper verb moved in front of the person doing it, and one was fetched when the sentence had none.
The first two words swapped places.
The word do was added because the sentence ends in a question mark.

teach.rule_line: To ask, move the helper. To refuse, put not after it. No helper? Use do.
teach.false_rule: That do is part of the question itself. It is not: it is the helper the sentence was missing, fetched in to be moved.

errors.wrong: Does the night bus stops at the harbour?
errors.right: Does the night bus stop at the harbour?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows one bus takes the ending and puts it on every verb in sight. Nothing tells them the helper has already taken it, so it is now marked twice.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on stops.

errors.wrong: The lifts doesn't work at weekends.
errors.right: The lifts don't work at weekends.
errors.why_it_happens: Doesn't has been stored as a single word meaning no, so the ending inside it stops being read as an ending and stops being checked against the doer.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: doesn't becomes don't.

errors.wrong: Rosa doesn't to work on Fridays.
errors.right: Rosa doesn't work on Fridays.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has met to in front of verbs after want and need and generalises it to anything that comes before a verb. A helper is the one place it never appears.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: Do you can open the office on a Sunday?
errors.right: Can you open the office on a Sunday?
errors.why_it_happens: Do has been learned as the way to start a question rather than as a stand-in for a missing helper, so it gets stacked on top of a helper the sentence already has.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: do.

pays_in.note: You cannot hold a conversation without asking anything, and every question runs on this.
pays_in.model: Do you get much of a lunch break where you work?

pays_in.note: A letter that asks for something politely is built on a moved helper.
pays_in.model: Could you confirm whether the caretaker holds a spare key?

pays_in.note: Helpers are the words speakers squash hardest, and missing one flips the answer.
pays_in.model: The office doesn't open until half past nine on a Monday.

used_in.quote: The examiner's questions on this card are all built this way, and a candidate who cannot hear the helper answers the wrong question.

payload.sentence: Lorna doesn't answer the desk phone after five.
payload.question: Will she pick up at half past five?

feedback.why_key: Not sits inside doesn't and cancels the whole of what follows it, including any hour after five.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for not inside the squashed helper.

payload.sentence: Does the night bus run on a Sunday?
payload.question: Does the speaker already know whether it runs?

feedback.why_key: A helper standing in front of the bus is English announcing that the speaker is missing something and would like it supplied.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a fronted helper as a request for information.

payload.context: Bea is asking about the new starter on the loading bay.
payload.sentence: Does she works on the early shift?
reasons: the ending is on the helper already, so the main verb should be plain
the new starter is not on the early shift
the question needs a different helper
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Does has already tied the sentence to one person. Putting the ending on works as well marks the same thing twice.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the ending off the main verb once a helper arrives.

payload.context: From an email to a community hall.
payload.stem: ___ the hall take bookings from outside the village?

feedback.why_key: The hall is one thing, so the helper that arrives to be moved takes the ending, and take stays plain behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the ending on the helper, never on both.

payload.context: Complaining about a block of flats.
payload.stem: The bins ___ (not empty) on a Bank Holiday and the caretaker ___ (not tell) anyone.

feedback.why_key: The bins are several and the caretaker is one, so the same move produces two different helpers in one sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the doers before you choose don't or doesn't.

payload.context: Ask somebody at the market entrance.

expected: do the stalls take cards on a weekday

feedback.why_key: The stalls are several, so the helper comes in plain, moves to the front, and leaves take exactly as it was.
feedback.feed_forward: Fetch the helper first, then move it.

payload.context: Write a line for a set of laboratory notes, in full words rather than short ones.

expected: the reading does not settle for an hour

feedback.why_key: Not goes straight after the helper and nowhere else, and settle behind it is plain because the helper is already carrying the ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Place not immediately after the helper every time.

payload.given: The college charges for the evening courses.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that it says the opposite, in full words rather than short ones.

expected: does not charge for the evening courses
doesn't charge for the evening courses
doesnt charge for the evening courses

feedback.why_key: There was no helper to put not after, so one was fetched, and the ending moved off charges onto it as it arrived.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the ending onto the helper as you fetch it.

points.title: Asking with what, who and where, and knowing when to leave do out

point_json.grammar_name: Wh- questions: subject questions and object questions

teach.can_do: I can ask about any part of a sentence, and I know which questions need do and which refuse it.
teach.why_it_matters: Almost nobody is taught that some questions take no do at all, so almost everybody puts one in and produces a question no listener would build.
teach.meaning: A question word stands in the hole where the missing information should be. Where that hole sits changes everything. If the hole is where the person or thing doing the verb would go, the question word simply fills it and the sentence keeps its ordinary shape: nothing has moved, so no helper is needed. If the hole is anywhere else, the question word jumps to the front, and the jump is what calls a helper in behind it.

form.pattern: question word + verb ...? when the hole is at the front; question word + helper + subject + plain verb ...? when it is not
notes: who, what and which can stand where the doer stands, and then no helper appears at all
when the hole is somewhere else, the question word goes to the front and do, does, is or can follows it
the ending stays on the verb in the first kind: who runs the desk, not who run the desk
why, when, where and how always leave the hole away from the doer, so they always take a helper
form.negative: Who doesn't sign the sheet? keeps the ordinary shape and still refuses a fronted helper.
form.question: Answer your own question with a name and see where the name lands.

points.title: Answering yes or no without repeating the whole sentence back

teach.can_do: I can answer a question in three words and say that the same is true of me.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between sounding like a person in a conversation and sounding like somebody reading a sentence back to the examiner.
teach.meaning: Once a question has been asked, everything in it is already on the table, so English throws almost all of it away and keeps two things: the person and the helper. That pair is enough to say yes or no, because the helper carries the time and the person carries the who. The same pair, turned round, says that something is true of you as well, which is how agreement is done without repeating a word of what was said.

form.pattern: Yes, + subject + helper. / No, + subject + helper + not.
notes: the helper must be the one the question used: are you ...? takes I am, do you ...? takes I do
the main verb never comes back: Yes, I do, never Yes, I do work
in the short yes there is no squashing: Yes, I am, not Yes, I'm
So + helper + subject says the same is true of me; Neither + helper + subject does it after a no
form.negative: No, + subject + helper + not, usually squashed: No, I don't. No, she isn't.
form.question: The question hands you the helper. Take it and hand it straight back.

points.title: Saying how often something happens, and putting the word where English keeps it

teach.can_do: I can say how often I do something and put the word in the slot English reserves for it.
teach.why_it_matters: The words are easy and the slot is not. A word in the wrong slot is the single most audible sign that a sentence was built rather than spoken.
teach.meaning: These words grade a habit rather than time it. They do not say when something happened; they say how much of the time it holds true, from all of it down to none of it. Because they measure the habit and not the event, English parks them beside the verb rather than at either end of the sentence, and the parking space is narrow: just ahead of an ordinary verb, just behind am, is and are.

form.pattern: subject + frequency word + verb, but subject + am / is / are + frequency word
notes: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, hardly ever and never fill the same slot
with a helper, the word goes between the helper and the main verb: I have never seen it
sometimes and usually may also start or end a sentence; always and never may not
never already carries the refusal, so the sentence takes no second one
form.negative: I don't often walk in. The word slips in after the helper and before the main verb.
form.question: Do you ever walk in? Ever is what these words become inside a question.

steps.gloss: every single time, with no exceptions
most times, and I would expect it
many times, but I would not bet on any one of them
here and there, with no pattern
hardly at all, and it is worth remarking on

worked_example.sentence: Lorna rarely takes the lift to the third floor.
worked_example.why_this_form: The word grades the habit, so it sits one step in front of the verb it is grading and nowhere else in the sentence.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Lorna takes rarely the lift puts the grading after the verb, where English keeps the thing the verb lands on, and the listener starts waiting for that thing instead.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic is always short of staff on a Monday.
notice_set.question: Is there an ordinary Monday when the clinic has enough staff?
notice_set.why: Always leaves no room at all, which is why it sits at the top of the scale and takes no exceptions.

notice_set.sentence: Bea sometimes walks the last mile home.
notice_set.question: Does she do it most days?
notice_set.why: Sometimes sits in the middle and refuses to say how far up or down it falls, which is exactly its job.

notice_set.sentence: I have never used the pool on a weekday.
notice_set.question: Has the speaker used the pool on a weekday?
notice_set.why: Never sits between the helper and the main verb, and it carries the whole refusal on its own.

teach.rule_line: One step in front of an ordinary verb; one step behind am, is and are.
teach.false_rule: That these words can go wherever they sound best, as they can in many languages. In English the slot is fixed and the ear notices when it is missed.

errors.wrong: I take always the stairs at work.
errors.right: I always take the stairs at work.
errors.why_it_happens: Most languages let a word like this follow the verb, and nothing in the meaning objects. It is a habit carried straight across, and it survives because the sentence is still perfectly clear.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: always goes in front of take.
errors.l1_note: Many languages place the adverb after the verb by default.

errors.wrong: Dev never is on time for the early class.
errors.right: Dev is never on time for the early class.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has drilled the slot in front of the verb and applies it to is as well. Nothing in the meaning marks is out as different, so the one exception is overwritten by the rule.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: never goes after is.

errors.wrong: Always I check the rota before I leave.
errors.right: I always check the rota before I leave.
errors.why_it_happens: Fronting the word feels emphatic and is normal in a good many languages. In English the front position is reserved, and always is one of the words that may not take it.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: always goes after I.

errors.wrong: My father never walk anywhere now.
errors.right: My father never walks anywhere now.
errors.why_it_happens: The frequency word sits between the doer and the verb, and by the time the learner reaches the verb the single father is two words behind and out of mind.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: s on walk.

pays_in.note: Almost every Part 1 question about your week is answered with one of these.
pays_in.model: I usually walk in, but I rarely bother in the winter.

pays_in.note: It softens a claim without weakening it, which is worth marks in an argument.
pays_in.model: Households in outer districts rarely have more than one bus an hour.

pays_in.note: A true-or-false stem that swaps usually for always is false on that word alone.
pays_in.model: Patients rarely wait more than a fortnight for a first appointment.

used_in.quote: How often do you do that? is on the card twice, and the answer needs the word in the right slot both times.

payload.sentence: Tamsin hardly ever misses a session.
payload.question: Is she at most sessions?

feedback.why_key: Hardly ever grades the missing, not the attending, so pushing the missing to the bottom pushes the attending to the top.
feedback.feed_forward: Check which verb the word is grading.

payload.sentence: The footbridge is often closed after heavy rain.
payload.question: Is it closed every time it rains hard?

feedback.why_key: Often sits well up the scale but stops short of the top, so it leaves the every-time claim unmade.
feedback.feed_forward: Read often as many, never as all.

payload.context: From a note about the yard routine.
payload.sentence: The supervisor checks always the load before it leaves.
reasons: the grading word is standing where the thing being checked should go
the supervisor does not check the load
the verb is missing its ending
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The slot straight after the verb belongs to whatever the verb lands on, so a reader arriving there is looking for the load and finds a grading word instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the grading word in front of the verb.

payload.context: Say when you go to the pool.

expected: i usually swim before the pool gets busy

feedback.why_key: One step in front of the verb, and everything about when and where waits until the verb has had its say.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the grading word between the person and the verb.

payload.context: Write one line for a report on adult education.

expected: evening classes are rarely full in the spring

feedback.why_key: Are is where the rule turns over: the grading word drops in behind it rather than in front, and that is the only exception to learn.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the grading word after are, is and am.

payload.context: From a leaflet about a walk-in clinic.
payload.stem: The clinic ___ (rarely / close) before six, and the pharmacy next door ___ (never / open) on a Sunday.

feedback.why_key: The grading word slips between the doer and the verb, and the verb still has to carry its ending because the clinic and the pharmacy are single things.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the ending to the verb even with a word in between.

payload.given: I have not eaten in that cafe. Not once.
payload.instruction: Say it in one sentence, using a single grading word to carry the refusal.

feedback.why_key: With a helper in the sentence the grading word takes the seat between it and the main verb, and never carries the whole refusal on its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the grading word between the helper and the verb.

payload.audio_text: She hardly ever takes the coast road in winter.

expected: she hardly ever takes the coast road in winter

feedback.why_key: Two small unstressed words sit between the person and the verb, and dropping either of them turns the sentence into its own opposite.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the words between the person and the verb first.

payload.sentence: Small firms reach never the size at which the grant becomes worth claiming.

feedback.why_key: The word is grading the reaching, so it belongs in front of it. Behind the verb it blocks the slot the size was heading for.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the grading word one step to the left.

payload.context: Dev is describing a Sunday at home.
payload.sentence: Always my mother cooks for whoever turns up.
reasons: this word cannot open the sentence and has to sit next to the verb
the mother does not cook on Sundays
the verb is missing its ending
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Sometimes and usually can open a sentence. Always and never cannot, and the front position is the one learners reach for when they want emphasis.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep always and never next to the verb, never at the front.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about how you get about in an ordinary week. Grade each habit with a different word, and use one sentence with am, is or are in it.

feedback.why_key: The sentence with am, is or are is the one that flips the slot, and writing both in a row is what fixes the flip in place.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the two slots side by side and compare them.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about free time. Answer three of its questions aloud in thirty seconds each, grading every habit rather than leaving it flat. Record it and check where each grading word landed.

feedback.why_key: At speaking speed the word drifts to wherever the sentence has room, which is usually behind the verb. A recording is where you can hear it drift.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen back and mark every grading word that landed late.

points.title: Saying that something is going on right now, or only for a while

teach.can_do: I can say that something is under way, and that it started and will stop.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shape that puts your listener at the scene, and it is also the shape learners spread onto sentences that have no scene in them at all.
teach.meaning: This shape stretches an event out and stands you inside it. It says that something has begun and has not finished, so it comes with two invisible edges: a start behind you and an end somewhere ahead. That is why it also fits arrangements that will not last and changes that are still under way. It is not a way of saying that something is happening close to now. It is a way of saying that it is unfinished.

notes: am with I, is with one person or one thing, are with you, we, they and any group
a verb ending in a single e drops it: make becomes making, take becomes taking
a short verb ending in one vowel and one consonant doubles the consonant: run becomes running
the ending goes on the main verb and the marking for who stays on am, is or are
form.negative: subject + am / is / are + not + verb + -ing
form.question: Am / Is / Are + subject + verb + -ing ...?

spec.caption: Not a dot near now, but a stretch with you inside it and an edge at either end.

worked_example.sentence: They are widening the lane outside the old market.
worked_example.why_this_form: The work has begun, it is not finished, and it will end. The shape puts the listener on the pavement watching it happen.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: They widen the lane would make it something the council does over and over, like emptying the bins, which would be an alarming thing to say about a lane.

notice_set.sentence: The shops on Verdon Road are losing trade.
notice_set.question: Has the loss finished?
notice_set.why: The stretch is still running, which is exactly what this shape is for: an edge behind and no edge reached yet.

notice_set.sentence: Rosa is staying with her cousin in Marlow.
notice_set.question: Has she moved to Marlow for good?
notice_set.why: The shape carries an ending somewhere ahead, so a permanent move is the one reading it rules out.

notice_set.sentence: The tide is coming in fast.
notice_set.question: Is the water still moving?
notice_set.why: You are placed inside the stretch, so the movement has not reached its far edge.

notice_set.sentence: Fewer people are learning a second language at school.
notice_set.question: Is the change finished?
notice_set.why: A change that is still under way takes the same shape as an action that is still under way, because it is the same idea.

notice_set.sentence: Omar is covering the late shift this fortnight.
notice_set.question: Is the late shift his usual arrangement?
notice_set.why: The shape puts an ending ahead of the arrangement, so it marks it as something other than the usual state of things.

teach.rule_line: Ask: has it begun and not yet finished?
teach.false_rule: That this shape means the present. It means unfinished, which is why it stretches over a fortnight or a decade just as happily as over a minute.

errors.wrong: The lorries is blocking the whole lane.
errors.right: The lorries are blocking the whole lane.
errors.why_it_happens: All the learner's attention is on getting the -ing ending onto the main verb, and the small word carrying the marking for who slips through unchecked.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: is becomes are.

errors.wrong: My sister working at the market on Saturdays.
errors.right: My sister is working at the market on Saturdays.
errors.why_it_happens: The -ing ending feels like the whole of the shape, because it is the visible part. Nothing in the meaning is lost when the small word in front of it goes missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: is.

errors.wrong: The council is emptying the bins on a Wednesday.
errors.right: The council empties the bins on a Wednesday.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner pictures the lorry and describes the picture. On a Wednesday names a repeating slot, and a repeating slot has no single stretch to stand inside.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is emptying becomes empties.

errors.wrong: They are runing the new service from the old depot.
errors.right: They are running the new service from the old depot.
errors.why_it_happens: The ending is bolted onto whatever letters are on the page. Short verbs built from one vowel and one closing consonant double that consonant first, and nothing on the page says so.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: a second n in running.

pays_in.note: A change still under way is the opening move of almost every essay about how life has altered.
pays_in.model: More of the old warehouses are being turned into flats every year.

pays_in.note: Describing a scene from your card puts the listener inside it.
pays_in.model: The whole street is being dug up while the pipes go in.

pays_in.note: The small word in front of the -ing is squashed almost to nothing, and it carries who.
pays_in.model: They're resurfacing the square while the market is still running.

used_in.quote: The card asks what is changing where you live, and a change under way takes this shape in every answer.

payload.sentence: The old mill is coming down brick by brick.
payload.question: Is the mill gone?

feedback.why_key: The sentence drops you into the middle of the work, and the far edge is still ahead, so part of the building has yet to come down.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the shape as unfinished, not as recent.

payload.sentence: Kester is working out of the Ashfield office for a few months.
payload.question: Is Ashfield where he is usually based?

feedback.why_key: The shape carries an ending somewhere ahead, which marks the arrangement as a detour rather than as the standing state of things.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the edge ahead before you decide it is permanent.

payload.context: Nell is telling a friend about her new flat.
payload.sentence: My brother helping me with the boxes.
reasons: the small word that carries who has gone missing
the brother is not helping
the ending on the verb is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing is only half the shape. Without is in front of it the sentence has an ending but nothing carrying who or when.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert am, is or are before every -ing verb.

payload.context: From a note on a building site at Brackenfield.
payload.stem: The contractors ___ (lay) the last of the pipes and the road ___ (settle) slowly.

feedback.why_key: Both stretches are open, and the small word in front changes because the contractors are several and the road is one.
feedback.feed_forward: Match am, is or are to the doer, then add -ing.

payload.context: Describing what is going on at home while you speak.
payload.stem: My cousin ___ (run) the shop while my aunt ___ (get) better.

feedback.why_key: Both verbs double their last letter before the ending, and both stretches have an edge ahead of them that nobody has reached.
feedback.feed_forward: Double the last letter of a short verb before adding -ing.

payload.context: Open a paragraph about the Verdon estuary.

expected: the estuary is silting up faster than expected

feedback.why_key: Silting is not an event so much as a drift, and a drift with no far edge behaves exactly like an unfinished action.
feedback.feed_forward: Use this shape for a change still under way.

payload.given: Bea started a course in September. She has not finished it.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that puts the listener inside the course with her.

expected: is doing a course at the moment

feedback.why_key: A start behind and no end reached is exactly the two edges this shape carries, so it fits without any extra word being needed.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for this shape when both edges are open.

payload.audio_text: They're widening the lane and the shops are losing trade.

expected: they're widening the lane and the shops are losing trade
they are widening the lane and the shops are losing trade
theyre widening the lane and the shops are losing trade

feedback.why_key: The opening pair squashes into a single beat, and that beat carries who is doing it as well as when, so losing it loses both.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the squashed beat before each -ing verb.

payload.sentence: The two ferries is running at half capacity while the slip is repaired.

feedback.why_key: Later in the sentence it goes right, because one slip is one thing. Two ferries needed the other small word and never got it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the doer for each small word separately.

items.decision_cue: most years since the mill shut

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a coastal economy.
payload.sentence: In most years since the mill shut, the town is losing about a hundred jobs.
reasons: most years names a repeating slot, and there is no single stretch to stand inside
the town has not lost any jobs
am, is or are has been chosen wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The shape needs one open stretch with you inside it. A run of separate years gives it a row of small stretches and nowhere to stand.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap to the plain verb when the sentence counts occasions.

payload.prompt_text: Something is being built or taken down where you live, and the work has not finished. Write two sentences that put a reader on the pavement watching it.

feedback.why_key: Unfinished work is the plainest case there is, and writing two sentences forces the small word in front to be marked twice.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the small word in front of each -ing verb.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about how your town has changed. Speak for forty seconds about what is changing there at present. Record it and check that every -ing verb kept its small word in front.

feedback.why_key: In speech the small word squashes down to almost nothing, and a word that quiet is the easiest one to leave out altogether.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen back and mark every -ing verb standing alone.

points.title: The verbs that refuse to be caught in the middle of happening

point_json.grammar_name: Stative verbs, and the ones that go both ways

teach.can_do: I can tell which verbs describe a state and leave them in their plain shape.
teach.why_it_matters: I am knowing and I am wanting are among the first errors a listener notices, and they set hard: learners produce them years after they can explain them.
teach.meaning: Some verbs do not name an event at all. They name how things stand: what you know, what you own, what something costs, what you think of it, what it looks like. A state has no middle to be caught in and no edges to stretch between, so the shape that stands you inside an unfinished stretch has nothing to work with. A handful of verbs describe both a state and an activity, and those switch meaning rather than switching shape.

form.pattern: state verbs stay in the plain shape: I know, she wants, it costs, they own
notes: knowing, understanding, believing, wanting, needing, preferring, owning, belonging: states, plain shape only
seeming, looking like, sounding like, costing, weighing, containing: states as well
think, have, see, taste, smell and expect describe a state in the plain shape and an activity in the other one
the plain shape here is not a habit. It is simply how things are.
form.negative: I don't know the answer, never I am not knowing the answer.
form.question: Do you want the last one? never Are you wanting the last one?

left.role: a state, with no middle to stand in
left.text: Ines knows the recipe by heart.

right.role: an activity, with a start and an end

spec.caption: Only the box on the right has a stretch in it. The box on the left is simply how things stand.

worked_example.sentence: Omar wants the corner table for the whole evening.
worked_example.why_this_form: Wanting is not something he starts and stops doing. It is how things stand with him, so there is no stretch for the other shape to stand inside.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Omar is wanting the table would try to catch him halfway through a wanting, and a listener cannot picture the halfway point of a want.

notice_set.sentence: This soup tastes of almost nothing.
notice_set.question: Is anybody doing anything to the soup?
notice_set.why: The sentence reports how the soup is, not an action performed on it, so nothing is under way at all.

notice_set.sentence: The chef is tasting the soup.
notice_set.question: Is anybody doing anything to the soup?
notice_set.why: The same verb has become an activity with a start and an end, and the shape has followed the meaning.

notice_set.sentence: Halima owns the bakery on the harbour road.
notice_set.question: Could she stop owning it in the next ten minutes?
notice_set.why: Owning is not a thing you do, so it cannot be paused, and a verb that cannot be paused has no middle to be caught in.

notice_set.sentence: The new oven costs more than the old one did.
notice_set.question: Is the oven doing anything?
notice_set.why: Costing is a fact about the oven rather than an activity of the oven, which is why the plain shape is the only one available.

notice_set.sentence: Dev is thinking about changing supplier.
notice_set.question: Has he made up his mind?
notice_set.why: Thinking here is an activity with a start and no end yet, which is a different verb from the one that reports an opinion.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same verb. What has changed between the left and the right?
pairs: This soup tastes of almost nothing.
The chef is tasting the soup.
Dev thinks the supplier is too slow.
Dev is thinking about changing supplier.
Halima has a bakery on the harbour road.
Halima is having a difficult month.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the verb reports how things stand; on the right it names something being done.
On the right the sentences are about the present and on the left they are about all time.
Verbs like taste, think and have never take the -ing shape.

teach.rule_line: If you could not stop it in ten minutes, you were not doing it. Use the plain shape.
teach.false_rule: That a list of forbidden verbs settles it. Half of them take both shapes, and what changes is the meaning, not the correctness.

contrast.question: Is this something being done, or a way things stand?

fork.answer: A way things stand: what you know, own, want, or what something costs or seems
Something being done, with a start behind it and an end ahead
A verb that does both, such as think, have, see or taste
fork.selects: either shape, and the meaning changes with it

a.text: Ines has lunch at the depot.
a.means: That is where her lunch happens as a matter of course.

b.text: Ines is having lunch at the depot.
b.means: She is at the table with the food in front of her.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Stretching a state verb does not produce a different meaning. It produces no meaning at all, because there is no halfway point of knowing something for a listener to picture, and they stall trying to find one.

edge_case.text: You will meet I'm loving this and I'm liking the new one in advertising and in casual speech. They are deliberate rule-breaks and they work because the rule is felt. They belong in a conversation and nowhere near an essay.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether you could stop doing it in the next ten minutes. If you cannot stop it, you were never doing it, and the plain shape is the only one on offer.

worked_pairs.a: Tamsin has the keys to the cold store.
worked_pairs.b: Tamsin is having trouble with the cold store.
worked_pairs.gloss: Holding keys is how things stand. Having trouble is something that started and will end, so the same verb takes two shapes.

worked_pairs.a: Omar sees the difficulty with the delivery slot.
worked_pairs.b: Omar is seeing the supplier about the delivery slot.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is understanding, which has no middle. The second is a meeting, which has a start, an end and a doorway.

worked_pairs.a: The stall smells of smoked fish.
worked_pairs.b: The inspector is smelling the fish before he signs it off.
worked_pairs.gloss: A stall is not doing anything. An inspector is, and you could interrupt him halfway through it.

errors.wrong: I am knowing the answer to that one.
errors.right: I know the answer to that one.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner wants to mark that this is true right at this moment and reaches for the shape that means right at this moment. Nothing warns them that knowing has no moment to be marked.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters and one word: am and the -ing.
errors.l1_note: Several languages allow the stretched shape with verbs of knowing and wanting.

errors.wrong: She is wanting a table for six on Friday.
errors.right: She wants a table for six on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The stretched shape has been learned as the polite or the current one, so it is used for anything happening around now, including things that are not happening at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is wanting becomes wants.

errors.wrong: The new oven is costing four hundred pounds.
errors.right: The new oven costs four hundred pounds.
errors.why_it_happens: A price feels like something happening in front of the learner, especially while they are looking at a label. Costing is a fact about the oven and the oven is doing nothing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is costing becomes costs.

errors.wrong: Dev thinks about changing supplier, so he has asked for three quotes.
errors.right: Dev is thinking about changing supplier, so he has asked for three quotes.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has over-learned the ban and applies it to think in both its meanings. Here think is an activity going on in his head, and the ban does not reach it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: thinks becomes is thinking.

pays_in.note: Opinions, preferences and what you own are all states, and Part 1 asks about all three.
pays_in.model: I prefer the market to the supermarket, mostly because I know the people there.

pays_in.note: An essay is full of what people believe, want and need, and every one of them is plain.
pays_in.model: Most households want a shorter journey more than they want a cheaper one.

pays_in.note: A passage switching a both-ways verb into the stretched shape has changed what it is claiming.
pays_in.model: The panel is seeing the applicants again before it makes a decision.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card is about what you like, what you know how to make and what you prefer, and none of them stretch.

payload.sentence: Nell prefers the bread from the corner stall.
payload.question: Is Nell doing something at this minute?

feedback.why_key: Preferring is how things stand with her, not an activity she is halfway through, so there is nothing to picture her doing.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether anybody is doing anything.

payload.sentence: The buyer is smelling the melons one by one.
payload.question: Could somebody interrupt her halfway through?

feedback.why_key: Somebody is doing something here, from the first melon to the last, and a job with a first and a last has a middle for the stretch to sit in.
feedback.feed_forward: Test for a halfway point before choosing the shape.

payload.context: Bea is ordering at the counter.
payload.sentence: I am wanting two of the small loaves, please.
reasons: wanting is not something anybody does, so it cannot be caught halfway
she does not want the loaves
the ending on the verb is misspelled
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The stretched shape asks a listener to picture her halfway through a wanting, and there is no such point to picture.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain shape for anything you cannot pause.

payload.context: From a note about a market stall.
payload.stem: The stall ___ (belong) to a family from Marlow and ___ (contain) more cheese than any shop in town.

feedback.why_key: Belonging and containing are both facts about the stall. Neither is anything the stall does, so neither can be stretched.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave a fact about a thing in the plain shape.

payload.context: Talking about a colleague who has stopped work to stare at a plan.
payload.stem: He ___ (think) about it and he ___ (know) the answer is somewhere in there.

feedback.why_key: One speaker, two verbs, two shapes: work is going on behind his eyes, while what he holds is simply held.
feedback.feed_forward: Split the sentence into what is happening and what holds.

payload.given: The price of the small ovens is being four hundred pounds.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that it says how much they cost, in as few words as possible.

feedback.why_key: A price belongs to the oven the way a weight does. The oven is not performing it, so the plain shape carries the whole report in one word.
feedback.feed_forward: Report a price with the plain verb only.

payload.context: Say who the flat above the shop belongs to.

expected: my grandmother owns the flat above the shop

feedback.why_key: Owning is not something she does between one hour and the next, so the verb stays plain and takes its ending for one person.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep verbs of owning and belonging plain.

payload.audio_text: I know the recipe, but I'm learning the timings.

expected: i know the recipe but i'm learning the timings
i know the recipe but i am learning the timings
i know the recipe but im learning the timings

feedback.why_key: One speaker, one sentence, two shapes: what she has is plain and what she is building takes the stretch.
feedback.feed_forward: Write each verb from what it claims, not from the speaker.

options.why_this_means: That the depot is where her lunch happens as a matter of course.

payload.stem: Kester ___ about the new rota.

points.title: Choosing between how things generally are and what is going on at the moment

teach.can_do: I can choose between the two present shapes on purpose, and say what the other one would have claimed.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the first choice in the course where both answers are correct English. What decides it is the situation, and getting it wrong says something you did not mean.
teach.meaning: The two shapes are not near and far from now. They are two different claims about the same stretch of time. The plain verb hands over the standing arrangement: how things are set up, what holds whether or not anyone is looking. The stretched shape puts your listener inside an unfinished period with an edge behind and an edge ahead. Same event, two claims: one about the arrangement, one about the stretch you are standing in.

form.pattern: subject + plain verb, against subject + am / is / are + verb + -ing
notes: the plain verb also covers timetables, rules, instructions and anything that repeats
the stretched shape also covers temporary arrangements and changes still under way
state verbs take only the plain shape, whatever the situation is
a whole paragraph should not drift between the two without a reason a reader can see

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this how it is set up, or something I am standing in the middle of?
teach.false_rule: That the plain verb is for habits and the stretched one is for now. A change under way runs for a decade and still takes the stretch.

contrast.question: Am I reporting the arrangement or standing inside an unfinished stretch?

fork.answer: The arrangement: how it is set up, what repeats, what a timetable or a rule says
An unfinished stretch: something under way, something temporary, something still changing
A state, such as knowing, owning, wanting or costing

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Stretching the verb over a permanent job does not sound broken. It sounds like a temporary posting, and your listener will ask when it ends. The wrong choice here produces a clear sentence saying something you never meant.

edge_case.text: The stretched shape with always is a complaint rather than a mistake: he is always leaving the gate open. It is standard, it is deliberate, and it belongs in speech rather than in an essay.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether the sentence would still be true in three years. If yes, the plain verb. If the honest answer is that it depends, you are inside a stretch.

points.title: Telling someone what to do, and inviting them to do it with you

teach.can_do: I can give an instruction in the fewest possible words, and suggest doing something together.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shortest sentence English has, it runs every set of instructions you will ever read, and it is the wrong shape for an argument.
teach.meaning: When you are speaking straight to somebody, both of you already know who is being addressed, so English throws the word for them away and starts with the verb. Nothing is missing: the person is the one you are looking at. Add let's in front and you put yourself into the instruction alongside them, which turns telling into suggesting without changing anything else about the sentence.

form.pattern: plain verb + the rest, with nobody named in front of it
notes: the verb is the plain shape, with no ending and nothing before it: Take the second turning
for the negative, put don't in front: Don't cross while the barrier is down
let's plus the plain verb includes you in it: Let's leave the boxes until Monday
please can go at the front or the end, and it softens without changing the shape
form.negative: Don't + plain verb, and Let's not + plain verb for the suggestion.
form.question: There is no question form. To ask rather than tell, use Could you + plain verb ...?

notice_set.why: Let's folds the speaker into the instruction, which is what turns telling somebody into suggesting to them.

notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking or telling?
notice_set.why: Please softens the edge on it, but the shape is still an instruction rather than a question.

notice_set.question: Is the writer telling the reader to do something?
notice_set.why: There is a named doer at the front, so the sentence argues about what somebody else ought to do rather than instructing the reader.

teach.rule_line: Start with the plain verb and name nobody. Put don't in front to refuse.
teach.false_rule: That leaving out the person is rude. It is the ordinary shape for instructions; naming them is what sounds odd.
